import Foundation.Vorspiel.Vorspiel

/-!
# Logic Symbols

This file defines structure that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$
and their homomorphisms.

## Main Definitions
* `LO.LogicalConnective` is defined so that `LO.LogicalConnective F` is a type that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$.
* `LO.LogicalConnective.Hom` is defined so that `f : F →ˡᶜ G` is a homomorphism from `F` to `G`, i.e.,
a function that preserves logical connectives.

-/

namespace LO

section logicNotation

@[notation_class] class Tilde (α : Type*) where
  tilde : α → α

@[notation_class] class Arrow (α : Type*) where
  arrow : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Wedge (α : Type*) where
  wedge : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Vee (α : Type*) where
  vee : α → α → α

class LogicalConnective (α : Type*)
  extends Top α, Bot α, Tilde α, Arrow α, Wedge α, Vee α

prefix:75 "∼" => Tilde.tilde

infixr:60 " ➝ " => Arrow.arrow

infixr:69 " ⋏ " => Wedge.wedge

infixr:68 " ⋎ " => Vee.vee

attribute [match_pattern]
  Tilde.tilde
  Arrow.arrow
  Wedge.wedge
  Vee.vee

end logicNotation

class DeMorgan (F : Type*) [LogicalConnective F] where
  verum           : ∼(⊤ : F) = ⊥
  falsum          : ∼(⊥ : F) = ⊤
  imply (φ ψ : F) : (φ ➝ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ψ
  and (φ ψ : F)   : ∼(φ ⋏ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ∼ψ
  or (φ ψ : F)    : ∼(φ ⋎ ψ) = ∼φ ⋏ ∼ψ
  neg (φ : F)     : ∼∼φ = φ

attribute [simp] DeMorgan.verum DeMorgan.falsum DeMorgan.and DeMorgan.or DeMorgan.neg

/-- Introducing `∼φ` as an abbreviation of `φ ➝ ⊥`. -/
class NegAbbrev (F : Type*) [Tilde F] [Arrow F] [Bot F] where
  neg {φ : F} : ∼φ = φ ➝ ⊥
-- attribute [simp] NegAbbrev.neg

namespace LogicalConnective

section
variable {α : Type*} [LogicalConnective α]

@[match_pattern] def iff (a b : α) := (a ➝ b) ⋏ (b ➝ a)

infix:61 " ⭤ " => LogicalConnective.iff

end

@[reducible]
instance PropLogicSymbols : LogicalConnective Prop where
  top := True
  bot := False
  tilde := Not
  arrow := fun P Q => (P → Q)
  wedge := And
  vee := Or

@[simp] lemma Prop.top_eq : ⊤ = True := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.bot_eq : ⊥ = False := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.neg_eq (φ : Prop) : ∼φ = ¬φ := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.arrow_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ➝ ψ) = (φ → ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.and_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⋏ ψ) = (φ ∧ ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.or_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⋎ ψ) = (φ ∨ ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.iff_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⭤ ψ) = (φ ↔ ψ) := by simp[LogicalConnective.iff, iff_iff_implies_and_implies]

instance : DeMorgan Prop where
  verum := by simp
  falsum := by simp
  imply := fun _ _ => by simp[imp_iff_not_or]
  and := fun _ _ => by simp[-not_and, not_and_or]
  or := fun _ _ => by simp[not_or]
  neg := fun _ => by simp

class HomClass (F : Type*) (α β : outParam Type*) [LogicalConnective α] [LogicalConnective β] [FunLike F α β] where
  map_top : ∀ (f : F), f ⊤ = ⊤
  map_bot : ∀ (f : F), f ⊥ = ⊥
  map_neg : ∀ (f : F) (φ : α), f (∼ φ) = ∼f φ
  map_imply : ∀ (f : F) (φ ψ : α), f (φ ➝ ψ) = f φ ➝ f ψ
  map_and : ∀ (f : F) (φ ψ : α), f (φ ⋏ ψ) = f φ ⋏ f ψ
  map_or  : ∀ (f : F) (φ ψ : α), f (φ ⋎ ψ) = f φ ⋎ f ψ

attribute [simp] HomClass.map_top HomClass.map_bot HomClass.map_neg HomClass.map_imply HomClass.map_and HomClass.map_or

namespace HomClass

variable (F : Type*) (α β : outParam Type*) [LogicalConnective α] [LogicalConnective β] [FunLike F α β]
variable [HomClass F α β]
variable (f : F) (a b : α)

instance : CoeFun F (fun _ => α → β) := ⟨DFunLike.coe⟩

@[simp] lemma map_iff : f (a ⭤ b) = f a ⭤ f b := by simp[LogicalConnective.iff]

end HomClass

variable (α β γ : Type*) [LogicalConnective α] [LogicalConnective β] [LogicalConnective γ]

structure Hom where
  toTr : α → β
  map_top' : toTr ⊤ = ⊤
  map_bot' : toTr ⊥ = ⊥
  map_neg' : ∀ φ, toTr (∼φ) = ∼toTr φ
  map_imply' : ∀ φ ψ, toTr (φ ➝ ψ) = toTr φ ➝ toTr ψ
  map_and' : ∀ φ ψ, toTr (φ ⋏ ψ) = toTr φ ⋏ toTr ψ
  map_or'  : ∀ φ ψ, toTr (φ ⋎ ψ) = toTr φ ⋎ toTr ψ

infix:25 " →ˡᶜ " => Hom
annotation: infix:25 " →ˡᶜ " => Hom

import Foundation.Vorspiel.Vorspiel

/-!
# Logic Symbols

This file defines structure that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$
and their homomorphisms.

## Main Definitions
* `LO.LogicalConnective` is defined so that `LO.LogicalConnective F` is a type that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$.
* `LO.LogicalConnective.Hom` is defined so that `f : F →ˡᶜ G` is a homomorphism from `F` to `G`, i.e.,
a function that preserves logical connectives.

-/

namespace LO

section logicNotation

@[notation_class] class Tilde (α : Type*) where
  tilde : α → α

@[notation_class] class Arrow (α : Type*) where
  arrow : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Wedge (α : Type*) where
  wedge : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Vee (α : Type*) where
  vee : α → α → α

class LogicalConnective (α : Type*)
  extends Top α, Bot α, Tilde α, Arrow α, Wedge α, Vee α

prefix:75 "∼" => Tilde.tilde

infixr:60 " ➝ " => Arrow.arrow

infixr:69 " ⋏ " => Wedge.wedge

infixr:68 " ⋎ " => Vee.vee

attribute [match_pattern]
  Tilde.tilde
  Arrow.arrow
  Wedge.wedge
  Vee.vee

end logicNotation

class DeMorgan (F : Type*) [LogicalConnective F] where
  verum           : ∼(⊤ : F) = ⊥
  falsum          : ∼(⊥ : F) = ⊤
  imply (φ ψ : F) : (φ ➝ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ψ
  and (φ ψ : F)   : ∼(φ ⋏ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ∼ψ
  or (φ ψ : F)    : ∼(φ ⋎ ψ) = ∼φ ⋏ ∼ψ
  neg (φ : F)     : ∼∼φ = φ

attribute [simp] DeMorgan.verum DeMorgan.falsum DeMorgan.and DeMorgan.or DeMorgan.neg

/-- Introducing `∼φ` as an abbreviation of `φ ➝ ⊥`. -/
class NegAbbrev (F : Type*) [Tilde F] [Arrow F] [Bot F] where
  neg {φ : F} : ∼φ = φ ➝ ⊥
-- attribute [simp] NegAbbrev.neg

namespace LogicalConnective

section
variable {α : Type*} [LogicalConnective α]

@[match_pattern] def iff (a b : α) := (a ➝ b) ⋏ (b ➝ a)

infix:61 " ⭤ " => LogicalConnective.iff

end

@[reducible]
instance PropLogicSymbols : LogicalConnective Prop where
  top := True
  bot := False
  tilde := Not
  arrow := fun P Q => (P → Q)
  wedge := And
  vee := Or

@[simp] lemma Prop.top_eq : ⊤ = True := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.bot_eq : ⊥ = False := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.neg_eq (φ : Prop) : ∼φ = ¬φ := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.arrow_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ➝ ψ) = (φ → ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.and_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⋏ ψ) = (φ ∧ ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.or_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⋎ ψ) = (φ ∨ ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.iff_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⭤ ψ) = (φ ↔ ψ) := by simp[LogicalConnective.iff, iff_iff_implies_and_implies]

instance : DeMorgan Prop where
  verum := by simp
  falsum := by simp
  imply := fun _ _ => by simp[imp_iff_not_or]
  and := fun _ _ => by simp[-not_and, not_and_or]

import Foundation.Vorspiel.Vorspiel

/-!
# Logic Symbols

This file defines structure that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$
and their homomorphisms.

## Main Definitions
* `LO.LogicalConnective` is defined so that `LO.LogicalConnective F` is a type that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$.
* `LO.LogicalConnective.Hom` is defined so that `f : F →ˡᶜ G` is a homomorphism from `F` to `G`, i.e.,
a function that preserves logical connectives.

-/

namespace LO

section logicNotation

@[notation_class] class Tilde (α : Type*) where
  tilde : α → α

@[notation_class] class Arrow (α : Type*) where
  arrow : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Wedge (α : Type*) where
  wedge : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Vee (α : Type*) where
  vee : α → α → α

class LogicalConnective (α : Type*)
  extends Top α, Bot α, Tilde α, Arrow α, Wedge α, Vee α

prefix:75 "∼" => Tilde.tilde

infixr:60 " ➝ " => Arrow.arrow

infixr:69 " ⋏ " => Wedge.wedge

infixr:68 " ⋎ " => Vee.vee

attribute [match_pattern]
  Tilde.tilde
  Arrow.arrow
  Wedge.wedge
  Vee.vee

end logicNotation

class DeMorgan (F : Type*) [LogicalConnective F] where
  verum           : ∼(⊤ : F) = ⊥
  falsum          : ∼(⊥ : F) = ⊤
  imply (φ ψ : F) : (φ ➝ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ψ
  and (φ ψ : F)   : ∼(φ ⋏ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ∼ψ
  or (φ ψ : F)    : ∼(φ ⋎ ψ) = ∼φ ⋏ ∼ψ
  neg (φ : F)     : ∼∼φ = φ

attribute [simp] DeMorgan.verum DeMorgan.falsum DeMorgan.and DeMorgan.or DeMorgan.neg

/-- Introducing `∼φ` as an abbreviation of `φ ➝ ⊥`. -/
class NegAbbrev (F : Type*) [Tilde F] [Arrow F] [Bot F] where
  neg {φ : F} : ∼φ = φ ➝ ⊥
-- attribute [simp] NegAbbrev.neg

namespace LogicalConnective

section
variable {α : Type*} [LogicalConnective α]

@[match_pattern] def iff (a b : α) := (a ➝ b) ⋏ (b ➝ a)

infix:61 " ⭤ " => LogicalConnective.iff

end

@[reducible]
instance PropLogicSymbols : LogicalConnective Prop where
  top := True
  bot := False
  tilde := Not
  arrow := fun P Q => (P → Q)
  wedge := And
  vee := Or

@[simp] lemma Prop.top_eq : ⊤ = True := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.bot_eq : ⊥ = False := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.neg_eq (φ : Prop) : ∼φ = ¬φ := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.arrow_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ➝ ψ) = (φ → ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.and_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⋏ ψ) = (φ ∧ ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.or_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⋎ ψ) = (φ ∨ ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.iff_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⭤ ψ) = (φ ↔ ψ) := by simp[LogicalConnective.iff, iff_iff_implies_and_implies]

instance : DeMorgan Prop where
  verum := by simp
  falsum := by simp

import Foundation.Vorspiel.Vorspiel

/-!
# Logic Symbols

This file defines structure that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$
and their homomorphisms.

## Main Definitions
* `LO.LogicalConnective` is defined so that `LO.LogicalConnective F` is a type that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$.
* `LO.LogicalConnective.Hom` is defined so that `f : F →ˡᶜ G` is a homomorphism from `F` to `G`, i.e.,
a function that preserves logical connectives.

-/

namespace LO

section logicNotation

@[notation_class] class Tilde (α : Type*) where
  tilde : α → α

@[notation_class] class Arrow (α : Type*) where
  arrow : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Wedge (α : Type*) where
  wedge : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Vee (α : Type*) where
  vee : α → α → α

class LogicalConnective (α : Type*)
  extends Top α, Bot α, Tilde α, Arrow α, Wedge α, Vee α

prefix:75 "∼" => Tilde.tilde

infixr:60 " ➝ " => Arrow.arrow

infixr:69 " ⋏ " => Wedge.wedge

infixr:68 " ⋎ " => Vee.vee

attribute [match_pattern]
  Tilde.tilde
  Arrow.arrow
  Wedge.wedge
  Vee.vee

end logicNotation

class DeMorgan (F : Type*) [LogicalConnective F] where
  verum           : ∼(⊤ : F) = ⊥
  falsum          : ∼(⊥ : F) = ⊤
  imply (φ ψ : F) : (φ ➝ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ψ
  and (φ ψ : F)   : ∼(φ ⋏ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ∼ψ
  or (φ ψ : F)    : ∼(φ ⋎ ψ) = ∼φ ⋏ ∼ψ
  neg (φ : F)     : ∼∼φ = φ

attribute [simp] DeMorgan.verum DeMorgan.falsum DeMorgan.and DeMorgan.or DeMorgan.neg

/-- Introducing `∼φ` as an abbreviation of `φ ➝ ⊥`. -/
class NegAbbrev (F : Type*) [Tilde F] [Arrow F] [Bot F] where
  neg {φ : F} : ∼φ = φ ➝ ⊥
-- attribute [simp] NegAbbrev.neg

namespace LogicalConnective

section
variable {α : Type*} [LogicalConnective α]

@[match_pattern] def iff (a b : α) := (a ➝ b) ⋏ (b ➝ a)

infix:61 " ⭤ " => LogicalConnective.iff

end

@[reducible]
instance PropLogicSymbols : LogicalConnective Prop where
  top := True
  bot := False
  tilde := Not
  arrow := fun P Q => (P → Q)
  wedge := And
  vee := Or

@[simp] lemma Prop.top_eq : ⊤ = True := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.bot_eq : ⊥ = False := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.neg_eq (φ : Prop) : ∼φ = ¬φ := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.arrow_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ➝ ψ) = (φ → ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.and_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⋏ ψ) = (φ ∧ ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.or_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⋎ ψ) = (φ ∨ ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.iff_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⭤ ψ) = (φ ↔ ψ) := by simp[LogicalConnective.iff, iff_iff_implies_and_implies]

instance : DeMorgan Prop where
  verum := by simp
  falsum := by simp
  imply := fun _ _ => by simp[imp_iff_not_or]
  and := fun _ _ => by simp[-not_and, not_and_or]
  or := fun _ _ => by simp[not_or]
  neg := fun _ => by simp

class HomClass (F : Type*) (α β : outParam Type*) [LogicalConnective α] [LogicalConnective β] [FunLike F α β] where
  map_top : ∀ (f : F), f ⊤ = ⊤
  map_bot : ∀ (f : F), f ⊥ = ⊥
  map_neg : ∀ (f : F) (φ : α), f (∼ φ) = ∼f φ
  map_imply : ∀ (f : F) (φ ψ : α), f (φ ➝ ψ) = f φ ➝ f ψ
  map_and : ∀ (f : F) (φ ψ : α), f (φ ⋏ ψ) = f φ ⋏ f ψ
  map_or  : ∀ (f : F) (φ ψ : α), f (φ ⋎ ψ) = f φ ⋎ f ψ

attribute [simp] HomClass.map_top HomClass.map_bot HomClass.map_neg HomClass.map_imply HomClass.map_and HomClass.map_or

namespace HomClass

import Foundation.Vorspiel.Vorspiel

/-!
# Logic Symbols

This file defines structure that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$
and their homomorphisms.

## Main Definitions
* `LO.LogicalConnective` is defined so that `LO.LogicalConnective F` is a type that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$.
* `LO.LogicalConnective.Hom` is defined so that `f : F →ˡᶜ G` is a homomorphism from `F` to `G`, i.e.,
a function that preserves logical connectives.

-/

namespace LO

section logicNotation

@[notation_class] class Tilde (α : Type*) where
  tilde : α → α

@[notation_class] class Arrow (α : Type*) where
  arrow : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Wedge (α : Type*) where
  wedge : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Vee (α : Type*) where
  vee : α → α → α

class LogicalConnective (α : Type*)
  extends Top α, Bot α, Tilde α, Arrow α, Wedge α, Vee α

prefix:75 "∼" => Tilde.tilde

infixr:60 " ➝ " => Arrow.arrow

infixr:69 " ⋏ " => Wedge.wedge

infixr:68 " ⋎ " => Vee.vee

attribute [match_pattern]
  Tilde.tilde
  Arrow.arrow
  Wedge.wedge
  Vee.vee

end logicNotation

class DeMorgan (F : Type*) [LogicalConnective F] where
  verum           : ∼(⊤ : F) = ⊥
  falsum          : ∼(⊥ : F) = ⊤
  imply (φ ψ : F) : (φ ➝ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ψ
  and (φ ψ : F)   : ∼(φ ⋏ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ∼ψ
  or (φ ψ : F)    : ∼(φ ⋎ ψ) = ∼φ ⋏ ∼ψ
  neg (φ : F)     : ∼∼φ = φ

attribute [simp] DeMorgan.verum DeMorgan.falsum DeMorgan.and DeMorgan.or DeMorgan.neg

/-- Introducing `∼φ` as an abbreviation of `φ ➝ ⊥`. -/
class NegAbbrev (F : Type*) [Tilde F] [Arrow F] [Bot F] where
  neg {φ : F} : ∼φ = φ ➝ ⊥
-- attribute [simp] NegAbbrev.neg

namespace LogicalConnective

section
variable {α : Type*} [LogicalConnective α]

@[match_pattern] def iff (a b : α) := (a ➝ b) ⋏ (b ➝ a)

infix:61 " ⭤ " => LogicalConnective.iff

end

@[reducible]
instance PropLogicSymbols : LogicalConnective Prop where
  top := True
  bot := False
  tilde := Not
  arrow := fun P Q => (P → Q)
  wedge := And
  vee := Or

@[simp] lemma Prop.top_eq : ⊤ = True := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.bot_eq : ⊥ = False := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.neg_eq (φ : Prop) : ∼φ = ¬φ := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.arrow_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ➝ ψ) = (φ → ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.and_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⋏ ψ) = (φ ∧ ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.or_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⋎ ψ) = (φ ∨ ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.iff_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⭤ ψ) = (φ ↔ ψ) := by simp[LogicalConnective.iff, iff_iff_implies_and_implies]

instance : DeMorgan Prop where
  verum := by simp
  falsum := by simp
  imply := fun _ _ => by simp[imp_iff_not_or]
  and := fun _ _ => by simp[-not_and, not_and_or]
  or := fun _ _ => by simp[not_or]
  neg := fun _ => by simp

class HomClass (F : Type*) (α β : outParam Type*) [LogicalConnective α] [LogicalConnective β] [FunLike F α β] where
  map_top : ∀ (f : F), f ⊤ = ⊤
  map_bot : ∀ (f : F), f ⊥ = ⊥
  map_neg : ∀ (f : F) (φ : α), f (∼ φ) = ∼f φ
  map_imply : ∀ (f : F) (φ ψ : α), f (φ ➝ ψ) = f φ ➝ f ψ
  map_and : ∀ (f : F) (φ ψ : α), f (φ ⋏ ψ) = f φ ⋏ f ψ
  map_or  : ∀ (f : F) (φ ψ : α), f (φ ⋎ ψ) = f φ ⋎ f ψ

attribute [simp] HomClass.map_top HomClass.map_bot HomClass.map_neg HomClass.map_imply HomClass.map_and HomClass.map_or

informal_statement: For any function \( f \) and any two disjoint sets \( s_1 \) and \( s_2 \), mapping \( f \) over their disjoint union is equivalent to mapping \( f \) over each set individually and then taking the disjoint union of those results.
informal_proof:
Let \( f \) be a function from \( \alpha \) to propositions, and let \( s_1 \) and \( s_2 \) be two disjoint subsets of \( \alpha \). We aim to show that mapping \( f \) over the disjoint union of \( s_1 \) and \( s_2 \) is the same as mapping \( f \) over each set individually and then taking their disjoint union.

First, consider an arbitrary element \( a \) that belongs to \( s_1 \cup s_2 \). Since \( s_1 \) and \( s_2 \) are disjoint, \( a \) must belong to either \( s_1 \) or \( s_2 \), but not both.

1. **Case 1:** If \( a \in s_1 \), then \( f(a) \) is included in \( f(s_1) \). Therefore, \( f(a) \) is also included in \( f(s_1) \) when considering \( f(s_1 \cup s_2) \), and in the disjoint union \( f(s_1) \disj f(s_2) \), \( f(a) \) is included because there’s no overlap between \( f(s_1) \) and \( f(s_2) \).

2. **Case 2:** Similarly, if \( a \in s_2 \), then \( f(a) \) is included in \( f(s_2) \), and hence in \( f(s_1 \cup s_2) \) and also in the disjoint union \( f(s_1) \disj f(s_2) \).

In both cases, the image of \( a \) under \( f \) is accounted for in both \( f(s_1 \cup s_2) \) and \( f(s_1) \disj f(s_2) \). Since this holds for any arbitrary element \( a \) in \( s_1 \cup s_2 \), the two sets \( f(s_1 \cup s_2) \) and \( f(s_1) \disj f(s_2) \) must be equal. Therefore, mapping \( f \) over a disjoint union of sets is equivalent to mapping \( f \) over each set individually and then taking their disjoint union.

import Foundation.Vorspiel.Vorspiel

/-!
# Logic Symbols

This file defines structure that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$
and their homomorphisms.

## Main Definitions
* `LO.LogicalConnective` is defined so that `LO.LogicalConnective F` is a type that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$.
* `LO.LogicalConnective.Hom` is defined so that `f : F →ˡᶜ G` is a homomorphism from `F` to `G`, i.e.,
a function that preserves logical connectives.

-/

namespace LO

section logicNotation

@[notation_class] class Tilde (α : Type*) where
  tilde : α → α

@[notation_class] class Arrow (α : Type*) where
  arrow : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Wedge (α : Type*) where
  wedge : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Vee (α : Type*) where
  vee : α → α → α

class LogicalConnective (α : Type*)
  extends Top α, Bot α, Tilde α, Arrow α, Wedge α, Vee α

prefix:75 "∼" => Tilde.tilde

infixr:60 " ➝ " => Arrow.arrow

infixr:69 " ⋏ " => Wedge.wedge

infixr:68 " ⋎ " => Vee.vee

attribute [match_pattern]
  Tilde.tilde
  Arrow.arrow
  Wedge.wedge
  Vee.vee

end logicNotation

class DeMorgan (F : Type*) [LogicalConnective F] where
  verum           : ∼(⊤ : F) = ⊥
  falsum          : ∼(⊥ : F) = ⊤
  imply (φ ψ : F) : (φ ➝ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ψ
  and (φ ψ : F)   : ∼(φ ⋏ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ∼ψ
  or (φ ψ : F)    : ∼(φ ⋎ ψ) = ∼φ ⋏ ∼ψ
  neg (φ : F)     : ∼∼φ = φ

attribute [simp] DeMorgan.verum DeMorgan.falsum DeMorgan.and DeMorgan.or DeMorgan.neg

/-- Introducing `∼φ` as an abbreviation of `φ ➝ ⊥`. -/
class NegAbbrev (F : Type*) [Tilde F] [Arrow F] [Bot F] where
  neg {φ : F} : ∼φ = φ ➝ ⊥
-- attribute [simp] NegAbbrev.neg

namespace LogicalConnective

section
variable {α : Type*} [LogicalConnective α]

@[match_pattern] def iff (a b : α) := (a ➝ b) ⋏ (b ➝ a)

infix:61 " ⭤ " => LogicalConnective.iff

end

@[reducible]
instance PropLogicSymbols : LogicalConnective Prop where
  top := True
  bot := False
  tilde := Not
  arrow := fun P Q => (P → Q)
  wedge := And
  vee := Or

@[simp] lemma Prop.top_eq : ⊤ = True := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.bot_eq : ⊥ = False := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.neg_eq (φ : Prop) : ∼φ = ¬φ := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.arrow_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ➝ ψ) = (φ → ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.and_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⋏ ψ) = (φ ∧ ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.or_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⋎ ψ) = (φ ∨ ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.iff_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⭤ ψ) = (φ ↔ ψ) := by simp[LogicalConnective.iff, iff_iff_implies_and_implies]

instance : DeMorgan Prop where
  verum := by simp
  falsum := by simp
  imply := fun _ _ => by simp[imp_iff_not_or]
  and := fun _ _ => by simp[-not_and, not_and_or]
  or := fun _ _ => by simp[not_or]
  neg := fun _ => by simp

class HomClass (F : Type*) (α β : outParam Type*) [LogicalConnective α] [LogicalConnective β] [FunLike F α β] where
  map_top : ∀ (f : F), f ⊤ = ⊤
  map_bot : ∀ (f : F), f ⊥ = ⊥
  map_neg : ∀ (f : F) (φ : α), f (∼ φ) = ∼f φ
  map_imply : ∀ (f : F) (φ ψ : α), f (φ ➝ ψ) = f φ ➝ f ψ
  map_and : ∀ (f : F) (φ ψ : α), f (φ ⋏ ψ) = f φ ⋏ f ψ
  map_or  : ∀ (f : F) (φ ψ : α), f (φ ⋎ ψ) = f φ ⋎ f ψ

attribute [simp] HomClass.map_top HomClass.map_bot HomClass.map_neg HomClass.map_imply HomClass.map_and HomClass.map_or

informal_statement: For a function \( f \) mapping from a type \(\alpha\) to propositions, the image of the disjunction of a finite set \( s \) is equivalent to the existence of an element in \( s \) that satisfies the proposition under \( f \).
informal_proof:
We can prove this by considering the definition of the image of a disjunction under a function. The image \( f(s.\text{disj}) \) consists of all propositions \( f(a) \) for \( a \) in \( s \). 

To show the equivalence \( f(s.\text{disj}) \leftrightarrow \exists a \in s, f(a) \), we note the following:

1. **Forward Direction**: If \( f(s.\text{disj}) \) holds, then \( f(a) \) must be true for some \( a \in s \) because the image includes all such \( f(a) \).

2. **Backward Direction**: If there exists an \( a \in s \) such that \( f(a) \) is true, then the disjunction \( s.\text{disj} \) is true, and thus \( f(s.\text{disj}) \) holds.

Since both directions rely on the existence of elements in \( s \) that make \( f(a) \) true, the equivalence is established.

import Foundation.Vorspiel.Vorspiel

/-!
# Logic Symbols

This file defines structure that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$
and their homomorphisms.

## Main Definitions
* `LO.LogicalConnective` is defined so that `LO.LogicalConnective F` is a type that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$.
* `LO.LogicalConnective.Hom` is defined so that `f : F →ˡᶜ G` is a homomorphism from `F` to `G`, i.e.,
a function that preserves logical connectives.

-/

namespace LO

section logicNotation

@[notation_class] class Tilde (α : Type*) where
  tilde : α → α

@[notation_class] class Arrow (α : Type*) where
  arrow : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Wedge (α : Type*) where
  wedge : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Vee (α : Type*) where
  vee : α → α → α

class LogicalConnective (α : Type*)
  extends Top α, Bot α, Tilde α, Arrow α, Wedge α, Vee α

prefix:75 "∼" => Tilde.tilde

infixr:60 " ➝ " => Arrow.arrow

infixr:69 " ⋏ " => Wedge.wedge

infixr:68 " ⋎ " => Vee.vee

attribute [match_pattern]
  Tilde.tilde
  Arrow.arrow
  Wedge.wedge
  Vee.vee

end logicNotation

class DeMorgan (F : Type*) [LogicalConnective F] where
  verum           : ∼(⊤ : F) = ⊥
  falsum          : ∼(⊥ : F) = ⊤
  imply (φ ψ : F) : (φ ➝ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ψ
  and (φ ψ : F)   : ∼(φ ⋏ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ∼ψ
  or (φ ψ : F)    : ∼(φ ⋎ ψ) = ∼φ ⋏ ∼ψ
  neg (φ : F)     : ∼∼φ = φ

attribute [simp] DeMorgan.verum DeMorgan.falsum DeMorgan.and DeMorgan.or DeMorgan.neg

/-- Introducing `∼φ` as an abbreviation of `φ ➝ ⊥`. -/
class NegAbbrev (F : Type*) [Tilde F] [Arrow F] [Bot F] where
  neg {φ : F} : ∼φ = φ ➝ ⊥
-- attribute [simp] NegAbbrev.neg

namespace LogicalConnective

section
variable {α : Type*} [LogicalConnective α]

@[match_pattern] def iff (a b : α) := (a ➝ b) ⋏ (b ➝ a)

infix:61 " ⭤ " => LogicalConnective.iff

end

@[reducible]
instance PropLogicSymbols : LogicalConnective Prop where
  top := True
  bot := False
  tilde := Not
  arrow := fun P Q => (P → Q)
  wedge := And
  vee := Or

@[simp] lemma Prop.top_eq : ⊤ = True := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.bot_eq : ⊥ = False := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.neg_eq (φ : Prop) : ∼φ = ¬φ := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.arrow_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ➝ ψ) = (φ → ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.and_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⋏ ψ) = (φ ∧ ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.or_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⋎ ψ) = (φ ∨ ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.iff_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⭤ ψ) = (φ ↔ ψ) := by simp[LogicalConnective.iff, iff_iff_implies_and_implies]

instance : DeMorgan Prop where
  verum := by simp
  falsum := by simp
  imply := fun _ _ => by simp[imp_iff_not_or]
  and := fun _ _ => by simp[-not_and, not_and_or]
  or := fun _ _ => by simp[not_or]
  neg := fun _ => by simp

class HomClass (F : Type*) (α β : outParam Type*) [LogicalConnective α] [LogicalConnective β] [FunLike F α β] where
  map_top : ∀ (f : F), f ⊤ = ⊤
  map_bot : ∀ (f : F), f ⊥ = ⊥
  map_neg : ∀ (f : F) (φ : α), f (∼ φ) = ∼f φ
  map_imply : ∀ (f : F) (φ ψ : α), f (φ ➝ ψ) = f φ ➝ f ψ
  map_and : ∀ (f : F) (φ ψ : α), f (φ ⋏ ψ) = f φ ⋏ f ψ
  map_or  : ∀ (f : F) (φ ψ : α), f (φ ⋎ ψ) = f φ ⋎ f ψ

attribute [simp] HomClass.map_top HomClass.map_bot HomClass.map_neg HomClass.map_imply HomClass.map_and HomClass.map_or

namespace HomClass

variable (F : Type*) (α β : outParam Type*) [LogicalConnective α] [LogicalConnective β] [FunLike F α β]
variable [HomClass F α β]
variable (f : F) (a b : α)

instance : CoeFun F (fun _ => α → β) := ⟨DFunLike.coe⟩

@[simp] lemma map_iff : f (a ⭤ b) = f a ⭤ f b := by simp[LogicalConnective.iff]

end HomClass

/-!
# Logic Symbols

This file defines structure that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$
and their homomorphisms.

## Main Definitions
* `LO.LogicalConnective` is defined so that `LO.LogicalConnective F` is a type that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$.
* `LO.LogicalConnective.Hom` is defined so that `f : F →ˡᶜ G` is a homomorphism from `F` to `G`, i.e.,
a function that preserves logical connectives.

-/

namespace LO

section logicNotation

@[notation_class] class Tilde (α : Type*) where
  tilde : α → α

@[notation_class] class Arrow (α : Type*) where
  arrow : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Wedge (α : Type*) where
  wedge : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Vee (α : Type*) where
  vee : α → α → α

class LogicalConnective (α : Type*)
  extends Top α, Bot α, Tilde α, Arrow α, Wedge α, Vee α

prefix:75 "∼" => Tilde.tilde

infixr:60 " ➝ " => Arrow.arrow

infixr:69 " ⋏ " => Wedge.wedge

infixr:68 " ⋎ " => Vee.vee

attribute [match_pattern]
  Tilde.tilde
  Arrow.arrow
  Wedge.wedge
  Vee.vee

end logicNotation

class DeMorgan (F : Type*) [LogicalConnective F] where
  verum           : ∼(⊤ : F) = ⊥
  falsum          : ∼(⊥ : F) = ⊤
  imply (φ ψ : F) : (φ ➝ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ψ
  and (φ ψ : F)   : ∼(φ ⋏ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ∼ψ
  or (φ ψ : F)    : ∼(φ ⋎ ψ) = ∼φ ⋏ ∼ψ
  neg (φ : F)     : ∼∼φ = φ

attribute [simp] DeMorgan.verum DeMorgan.falsum DeMorgan.and DeMorgan.or DeMorgan.neg

/-- Introducing `∼φ` as an abbreviation of `φ ➝ ⊥`. -/
class NegAbbrev (F : Type*) [Tilde F] [Arrow F] [Bot F] where
  neg {φ : F} : ∼φ = φ ➝ ⊥
-- attribute [simp] NegAbbrev.neg

namespace LogicalConnective

section
variable {α : Type*} [LogicalConnective α]

@[match_pattern] def iff (a b : α) := (a ➝ b) ⋏ (b ➝ a)

infix:61 " ⭤ " => LogicalConnective.iff

end

@[reducible]
instance PropLogicSymbols : LogicalConnective Prop where
  top := True
  bot := False
  tilde := Not
  arrow := fun P Q => (P → Q)
  wedge := And
  vee := Or

@[simp] lemma Prop.top_eq : ⊤ = True := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.bot_eq : ⊥ = False := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.neg_eq (φ : Prop) : ∼φ = ¬φ := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.arrow_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ➝ ψ) = (φ → ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.and_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⋏ ψ) = (φ ∧ ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.or_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⋎ ψ) = (φ ∨ ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.iff_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⭤ ψ) = (φ ↔ ψ) := by simp[LogicalConnective.iff, iff_iff_implies_and_implies]

instance : DeMorgan Prop where
  verum := by simp
  falsum := by simp
  imply := fun _ _ => by simp[imp_iff_not_or]
  and := fun _ _ => by simp[-not_and, not_and_or]
  or := fun _ _ => by simp[not_or]
  neg := fun _ => by simp

  map_and : ∀ (f : F) (φ ψ : α), f (φ ⋏ ψ) = f φ ⋏ f ψ
  map_or  : ∀ (f : F) (φ ψ : α), f (φ ⋎ ψ) = f φ ⋎ f ψ

attribute [simp] HomClass.map_top HomClass.map_bot HomClass.map_neg HomClass.map_imply HomClass.map_and HomClass.map_or

# Logic Symbols

This file defines structure that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$
and their homomorphisms.

## Main Definitions
* `LO.LogicalConnective` is defined so that `LO.LogicalConnective F` is a type that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$.
* `LO.LogicalConnective.Hom` is defined so that `f : F →ˡᶜ G` is a homomorphism from `F` to `G`, i.e.,
a function that preserves logical connectives.

-/

namespace LO

section logicNotation

@[notation_class] class Tilde (α : Type*) where
  tilde : α → α

@[notation_class] class Arrow (α : Type*) where
  arrow : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Wedge (α : Type*) where
  wedge : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Vee (α : Type*) where
  vee : α → α → α

class LogicalConnective (α : Type*)
  extends Top α, Bot α, Tilde α, Arrow α, Wedge α, Vee α

prefix:75 "∼" => Tilde.tilde

infixr:69 " ⋏ " => Wedge.wedge

infixr:68 " ⋎ " => Vee.vee

attribute [match_pattern]
  Tilde.tilde
  Arrow.arrow
  Wedge.wedge
  Vee.vee

end logicNotation

class DeMorgan (F : Type*) [LogicalConnective F] where
  verum           : ∼(⊤ : F) = ⊥
  falsum          : ∼(⊥ : F) = ⊤
  imply (φ ψ : F) : (φ ➝ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ψ
  and (φ ψ : F)   : ∼(φ ⋏ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ∼ψ
  or (φ ψ : F)    : ∼(φ ⋎ ψ) = ∼φ ⋏ ∼ψ
  neg (φ : F)     : ∼∼φ = φ

  neg {φ : F} : ∼φ = φ ➝ ⊥
-- attribute [simp] NegAbbrev.neg

instance PropLogicSymbols : LogicalConnective Prop where
  top := True
  bot := False

  arrow := fun P Q => (P → Q)
  wedge := And
  vee := Or

@[simp] lemma Prop.bot_eq : ⊥ = False := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.neg_eq (φ : Prop) : ∼φ = ¬φ := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.and_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⋏ ψ) = (φ ∧ ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.or_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⋎ ψ) = (φ ∨ ψ) := rfl

  or := fun _ _ => by simp[not_or]
  neg := fun _ => by simp

  map_and : ∀ (f : F) (φ ψ : α), f (φ ⋏ ψ) = f φ ⋏ f ψ
  map_or  : ∀ (f : F) (φ ψ : α), f (φ ⋎ ψ) = f φ ⋎ f ψ

attribute [simp] HomClass.map_top HomClass.map_bot HomClass.map_neg HomClass.map_imply HomClass.map_and HomClass.map_or

informal_statement: For any function \( f \) that maps elements from a type \( \alpha \) to propositions, the conjunction (logical "and") of \( f \) applied over all elements of a finite set \( s \) is equivalent to the conjunction of \( f \) applied to each individual element of \( s \).
informal_proof:
To understand this lemma, consider that \( s \) is a finite set of elements from \( \alpha \), and \( f \) is a function that takes each element of \( \alpha \) and returns a proposition. The notation \( s.\text{conj} \) represents the logical conjunction of all elements in \( s \). When we apply \( f \) to \( s.\text{conj} \), it means we are applying \( f \) to this combined conjunction.

On the other hand, \( \forall a \in s, f(a) \) signifies that for every element \( a \) in \( s \), the proposition \( f(a) \) holds. The lemma asserts that these two expressions are equivalent, i.e., \( f(s.\text{conj}) \) is equivalent to \( \forall a \in s, f(a) \).

To see why this equivalence holds, consider breaking down \( s \) into its constituent elements (using \( s.\text{toList} \)). Applying \( f \) to each element of the list and then combining them with conjunction (as in \( \text{List.map_conj} \)) yields the same result as applying \( f \) directly to the conjunction of all elements in \( s \). This is because both processes ensure that \( f \) is evaluated for each individual element, preserving the logical structure of the conjunction.

Therefore, whether you first combine all elements of \( s \) into a single conjunction and then apply \( f \), or you apply \( f \) to each element and then combine those results with conjunction, the outcome is the same. This equivalence holds true because the function \( f \) operates uniformly across all elements of the set, maintaining the logical integrity of the conjunction.

import Foundation.Vorspiel.Vorspiel

/-!
# Logic Symbols

This file defines structure that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$
and their homomorphisms.

## Main Definitions
* `LO.LogicalConnective` is defined so that `LO.LogicalConnective F` is a type that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$.
* `LO.LogicalConnective.Hom` is defined so that `f : F →ˡᶜ G` is a homomorphism from `F` to `G`, i.e.,
a function that preserves logical connectives.

-/

namespace LO

section logicNotation

@[notation_class] class Tilde (α : Type*) where
  tilde : α → α

@[notation_class] class Arrow (α : Type*) where
  arrow : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Wedge (α : Type*) where
  wedge : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Vee (α : Type*) where
  vee : α → α → α

class LogicalConnective (α : Type*)
  extends Top α, Bot α, Tilde α, Arrow α, Wedge α, Vee α

  Arrow.arrow

end logicNotation

class DeMorgan (F : Type*) [LogicalConnective F] where
  verum           : ∼(⊤ : F) = ⊥
  falsum          : ∼(⊥ : F) = ⊤
  imply (φ ψ : F) : (φ ➝ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ψ
  and (φ ψ : F)   : ∼(φ ⋏ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ∼ψ
  or (φ ψ : F)    : ∼(φ ⋎ ψ) = ∼φ ⋏ ∼ψ
  neg (φ : F)     : ∼∼φ = φ

attribute [simp] DeMorgan.verum DeMorgan.falsum DeMorgan.and DeMorgan.or DeMorgan.neg

/-- Introducing `∼φ` as an abbreviation of `φ ➝ ⊥`. -/
class NegAbbrev (F : Type*) [Tilde F] [Arrow F] [Bot F] where
  neg {φ : F} : ∼φ = φ ➝ ⊥

namespace LogicalConnective

section
variable {α : Type*} [LogicalConnective α]

@[match_pattern] def iff (a b : α) := (a ➝ b) ⋏ (b ➝ a)

@[reducible]
instance PropLogicSymbols : LogicalConnective Prop where
  top := True
  bot := False
  tilde := Not
  arrow := fun P Q => (P → Q)
  wedge := And
  vee := Or

@[simp] lemma Prop.top_eq : ⊤ = True := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.bot_eq : ⊥ = False := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.neg_eq (φ : Prop) : ∼φ = ¬φ := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.arrow_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ➝ ψ) = (φ → ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.and_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⋏ ψ) = (φ ∧ ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.or_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⋎ ψ) = (φ ∨ ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.iff_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⭤ ψ) = (φ ↔ ψ) := by simp[LogicalConnective.iff, iff_iff_implies_and_implies]

instance : DeMorgan Prop where
  verum := by simp
  falsum := by simp
  imply := fun _ _ => by simp[imp_iff_not_or]
  and := fun _ _ => by simp[-not_and, not_and_or]
  or := fun _ _ => by simp[not_or]
  neg := fun _ => by simp

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
Gadget for marking output parameters in type classes.

For example, the `Membership` class is defined as:
```
class Membership (α : outParam (Type u)) (γ : Type v)
```
This means that whenever a typeclass goal of the form `Membership ?α ?γ` comes
up, Lean will wait to solve it until `?γ` is known, but then it will run
typeclass inference, and take the first solution it finds, for any value of `?α`,
which thereby determines what `?α` should be.

This expresses that in a term like `a ∈ s`, `s` might be a `Set α` or
`List α` or some other type with a membership operation, and in each case
the "member" type `α` is determined by looking at the container type.
-/
@[reducible] def outParam (α : Sort u) : Sort u := α

import Foundation.Vorspiel.Vorspiel

/-!
# Logic Symbols

This file defines structure that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$
and their homomorphisms.

## Main Definitions
* `LO.LogicalConnective` is defined so that `LO.LogicalConnective F` is a type that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$.
* `LO.LogicalConnective.Hom` is defined so that `f : F →ˡᶜ G` is a homomorphism from `F` to `G`, i.e.,
a function that preserves logical connectives.

-/

namespace LO

section logicNotation

@[notation_class] class Tilde (α : Type*) where
  tilde : α → α

@[notation_class] class Arrow (α : Type*) where
  arrow : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Wedge (α : Type*) where
  wedge : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Vee (α : Type*) where
  vee : α → α → α

class LogicalConnective (α : Type*)
  extends Top α, Bot α, Tilde α, Arrow α, Wedge α, Vee α

prefix:75 "∼" => Tilde.tilde

infixr:60 " ➝ " => Arrow.arrow

infixr:69 " ⋏ " => Wedge.wedge

infixr:68 " ⋎ " => Vee.vee

attribute [match_pattern]
  Tilde.tilde
  Arrow.arrow
  Wedge.wedge
  Vee.vee

end logicNotation

class DeMorgan (F : Type*) [LogicalConnective F] where
  verum           : ∼(⊤ : F) = ⊥
  falsum          : ∼(⊥ : F) = ⊤
  imply (φ ψ : F) : (φ ➝ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ψ
  and (φ ψ : F)   : ∼(φ ⋏ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ∼ψ
  or (φ ψ : F)    : ∼(φ ⋎ ψ) = ∼φ ⋏ ∼ψ
  neg (φ : F)     : ∼∼φ = φ

attribute [simp] DeMorgan.verum DeMorgan.falsum DeMorgan.and DeMorgan.or DeMorgan.neg

/-- Introducing `∼φ` as an abbreviation of `φ ➝ ⊥`. -/
class NegAbbrev (F : Type*) [Tilde F] [Arrow F] [Bot F] where
  neg {φ : F} : ∼φ = φ ➝ ⊥
-- attribute [simp] NegAbbrev.neg

namespace LogicalConnective

section
variable {α : Type*} [LogicalConnective α]

@[match_pattern] def iff (a b : α) := (a ➝ b) ⋏ (b ➝ a)

infix:61 " ⭤ " => LogicalConnective.iff

end

@[reducible]
instance PropLogicSymbols : LogicalConnective Prop where
  top := True
  bot := False
  tilde := Not
  arrow := fun P Q => (P → Q)
  wedge := And
  vee := Or

@[simp] lemma Prop.top_eq : ⊤ = True := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.bot_eq : ⊥ = False := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.neg_eq (φ : Prop) : ∼φ = ¬φ := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.arrow_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ➝ ψ) = (φ → ψ) := rfl

C1_dependencies.name: outParam
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
Gadget for marking output parameters in type classes.

For example, the `Membership` class is defined as:
```
class Membership (α : outParam (Type u)) (γ : Type v)
```
This means that whenever a typeclass goal of the form `Membership ?α ?γ` comes
up, Lean will wait to solve it until `?γ` is known, but then it will run
typeclass inference, and take the first solution it finds, for any value of `?α`,
which thereby determines what `?α` should be.

This expresses that in a term like `a ∈ s`, `s` might be a `Set α` or
`List α` or some other type with a membership operation, and in each case
the "member" type `α` is determined by looking at the container type.
-/
@[reducible] def outParam (α : Sort u) : Sort u := α

import Foundation.Vorspiel.Vorspiel

/-!
# Logic Symbols

This file defines structure that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$
and their homomorphisms.

## Main Definitions
* `LO.LogicalConnective` is defined so that `LO.LogicalConnective F` is a type that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$.
* `LO.LogicalConnective.Hom` is defined so that `f : F →ˡᶜ G` is a homomorphism from `F` to `G`, i.e.,
a function that preserves logical connectives.

-/

namespace LO

section logicNotation

@[notation_class] class Tilde (α : Type*) where
  tilde : α → α

@[notation_class] class Arrow (α : Type*) where
  arrow : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Wedge (α : Type*) where
  wedge : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Vee (α : Type*) where
  vee : α → α → α

class LogicalConnective (α : Type*)
  extends Top α, Bot α, Tilde α, Arrow α, Wedge α, Vee α

prefix:75 "∼" => Tilde.tilde

infixr:60 " ➝ " => Arrow.arrow

infixr:69 " ⋏ " => Wedge.wedge

infixr:68 " ⋎ " => Vee.vee

attribute [match_pattern]
  Tilde.tilde
  Arrow.arrow
  Wedge.wedge
  Vee.vee

end logicNotation

class DeMorgan (F : Type*) [LogicalConnective F] where
  verum           : ∼(⊤ : F) = ⊥
  falsum          : ∼(⊥ : F) = ⊤
  imply (φ ψ : F) : (φ ➝ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ψ
  and (φ ψ : F)   : ∼(φ ⋏ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ∼ψ
  or (φ ψ : F)    : ∼(φ ⋎ ψ) = ∼φ ⋏ ∼ψ
  neg (φ : F)     : ∼∼φ = φ

attribute [simp] DeMorgan.verum DeMorgan.falsum DeMorgan.and DeMorgan.or DeMorgan.neg

/-- Introducing `∼φ` as an abbreviation of `φ ➝ ⊥`. -/
class NegAbbrev (F : Type*) [Tilde F] [Arrow F] [Bot F] where
  neg {φ : F} : ∼φ = φ ➝ ⊥
-- attribute [simp] NegAbbrev.neg

namespace LogicalConnective

section
variable {α : Type*} [LogicalConnective α]

@[match_pattern] def iff (a b : α) := (a ➝ b) ⋏ (b ➝ a)

infix:61 " ⭤ " => LogicalConnective.iff

end

@[reducible]
instance PropLogicSymbols : LogicalConnective Prop where
  top := True
  bot := False
  tilde := Not
  arrow := fun P Q => (P → Q)
  wedge := And
  vee := Or

@[simp] lemma Prop.top_eq : ⊤ = True := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.bot_eq : ⊥ = False := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.neg_eq (φ : Prop) : ∼φ = ¬φ := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.arrow_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ➝ ψ) = (φ → ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.and_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⋏ ψ) = (φ ∧ ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.iff_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⭤ ψ) = (φ ↔ ψ) := by simp[LogicalConnective.iff, iff_iff_implies_and_implies]

instance : DeMorgan Prop where

  and := fun _ _ => by simp[-not_and, not_and_or]

/--
Gadget for marking output parameters in type classes.

For example, the `Membership` class is defined as:
```
class Membership (α : outParam (Type u)) (γ : Type v)
```
This means that whenever a typeclass goal of the form `Membership ?α ?γ` comes
up, Lean will wait to solve it until `?γ` is known, but then it will run
typeclass inference, and take the first solution it finds, for any value of `?α`,
which thereby determines what `?α` should be.

This expresses that in a term like `a ∈ s`, `s` might be a `Set α` or
`List α` or some other type with a membership operation, and in each case
the "member" type `α` is determined by looking at the container type.
-/
@[reducible] def outParam (α : Sort u) : Sort u := α

informal_statement: For any propositions $a$ and $b$, the conjunction $a \land b$ is equivalent to $b \land a$. In other words, the order of propositions in a conjunction does not affect its truth value.
informal_proof:
First, let us assume that $a \land b$ is true. By the definition of conjunction, this means that both $a$ and $b$ are true. Since the order of stating the truth values does not change the overall truth value, $b \land a$ is also true. This establishes the forward direction of the equivalence.

Conversely, if $b \land a$ is true, then both $b$ and $a$ are true. Again, since the order of stating the truth values does not affect the overall truth value, $a \land b$ is also true. This establishes the reverse direction of the equivalence.

Therefore, $a \land b$ is equivalent to $b \land a$.

import Foundation.Vorspiel.Vorspiel

/-!
# Logic Symbols

This file defines structure that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$
and their homomorphisms.

## Main Definitions
* `LO.LogicalConnective` is defined so that `LO.LogicalConnective F` is a type that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$.
* `LO.LogicalConnective.Hom` is defined so that `f : F →ˡᶜ G` is a homomorphism from `F` to `G`, i.e.,
a function that preserves logical connectives.

-/

namespace LO

section logicNotation

@[notation_class] class Tilde (α : Type*) where
  tilde : α → α

@[notation_class] class Arrow (α : Type*) where
  arrow : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Wedge (α : Type*) where
  wedge : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Vee (α : Type*) where
  vee : α → α → α

class LogicalConnective (α : Type*)
  extends Top α, Bot α, Tilde α, Arrow α, Wedge α, Vee α

  Arrow.arrow

  Vee.vee

end logicNotation

class DeMorgan (F : Type*) [LogicalConnective F] where
  verum           : ∼(⊤ : F) = ⊥
  falsum          : ∼(⊥ : F) = ⊤
  imply (φ ψ : F) : (φ ➝ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ψ
  and (φ ψ : F)   : ∼(φ ⋏ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ∼ψ
  or (φ ψ : F)    : ∼(φ ⋎ ψ) = ∼φ ⋏ ∼ψ
  neg (φ : F)     : ∼∼φ = φ

attribute [simp] DeMorgan.verum DeMorgan.falsum DeMorgan.and DeMorgan.or DeMorgan.neg

/-- Introducing `∼φ` as an abbreviation of `φ ➝ ⊥`. -/
class NegAbbrev (F : Type*) [Tilde F] [Arrow F] [Bot F] where
  neg {φ : F} : ∼φ = φ ➝ ⊥

section
variable {α : Type*} [LogicalConnective α]

@[match_pattern] def iff (a b : α) := (a ➝ b) ⋏ (b ➝ a)

infix:61 " ⭤ " => LogicalConnective.iff

@[reducible]
instance PropLogicSymbols : LogicalConnective Prop where
  top := True
  bot := False
  tilde := Not
  arrow := fun P Q => (P → Q)
  wedge := And
  vee := Or

@[simp] lemma Prop.top_eq : ⊤ = True := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.bot_eq : ⊥ = False := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.neg_eq (φ : Prop) : ∼φ = ¬φ := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.arrow_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ➝ ψ) = (φ → ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.and_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⋏ ψ) = (φ ∧ ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.or_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⋎ ψ) = (φ ∨ ψ) := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.iff_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⭤ ψ) = (φ ↔ ψ) := by simp[LogicalConnective.iff, iff_iff_implies_and_implies]

instance : DeMorgan Prop where
  verum := by simp
  falsum := by simp
  imply := fun _ _ => by simp[imp_iff_not_or]
  and := fun _ _ => by simp[-not_and, not_and_or]
  or := fun _ _ => by simp[not_or]
  neg := fun _ => by simp

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
Gadget for marking output parameters in type classes.

For example, the `Membership` class is defined as:
```
class Membership (α : outParam (Type u)) (γ : Type v)
```
This means that whenever a typeclass goal of the form `Membership ?α ?γ` comes
up, Lean will wait to solve it until `?γ` is known, but then it will run
typeclass inference, and take the first solution it finds, for any value of `?α`,
which thereby determines what `?α` should be.

This expresses that in a term like `a ∈ s`, `s` might be a `Set α` or
`List α` or some other type with a membership operation, and in each case
the "member" type `α` is determined by looking at the container type.
-/
@[reducible] def outParam (α : Sort u) : Sort u := α

informal_statement: The disjunction of a set containing a single proposition φ is equivalent to φ itself.
informal_proof:
First, we consider the set that contains only one proposition, φ.

The disjunction of such a set is essentially asking whether any of the propositions in the set are true. Since there's only one proposition in this set, we're effectively asking whether φ is true.

Therefore, the disjunction over the set containing only φ is exactly φ.

This demonstrates that ⋁[φ] = φ, as the disjunction of a singleton set {φ} amounts to φ itself.

import Foundation.Vorspiel.Vorspiel

/-!
# Logic Symbols

This file defines structure that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$
and their homomorphisms.

## Main Definitions
* `LO.LogicalConnective` is defined so that `LO.LogicalConnective F` is a type that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$.
* `LO.LogicalConnective.Hom` is defined so that `f : F →ˡᶜ G` is a homomorphism from `F` to `G`, i.e.,
a function that preserves logical connectives.

-/

namespace LO

section logicNotation

@[notation_class] class Tilde (α : Type*) where
  tilde : α → α

@[notation_class] class Arrow (α : Type*) where
  arrow : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Wedge (α : Type*) where
  wedge : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Vee (α : Type*) where
  vee : α → α → α

class LogicalConnective (α : Type*)
  extends Top α, Bot α, Tilde α, Arrow α, Wedge α, Vee α

prefix:75 "∼" => Tilde.tilde

infixr:60 " ➝ " => Arrow.arrow

infixr:69 " ⋏ " => Wedge.wedge

infixr:68 " ⋎ " => Vee.vee

attribute [match_pattern]
  Tilde.tilde
  Arrow.arrow
  Wedge.wedge
  Vee.vee

end logicNotation

class DeMorgan (F : Type*) [LogicalConnective F] where
  verum           : ∼(⊤ : F) = ⊥
  falsum          : ∼(⊥ : F) = ⊤
  imply (φ ψ : F) : (φ ➝ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ψ
  and (φ ψ : F)   : ∼(φ ⋏ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ∼ψ
  or (φ ψ : F)    : ∼(φ ⋎ ψ) = ∼φ ⋏ ∼ψ
  neg (φ : F)     : ∼∼φ = φ

attribute [simp] DeMorgan.verum DeMorgan.falsum DeMorgan.and DeMorgan.or DeMorgan.neg

C1_dependencies.name: outParam
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
Gadget for marking output parameters in type classes.

For example, the `Membership` class is defined as:
```
class Membership (α : outParam (Type u)) (γ : Type v)
```
This means that whenever a typeclass goal of the form `Membership ?α ?γ` comes
up, Lean will wait to solve it until `?γ` is known, but then it will run
typeclass inference, and take the first solution it finds, for any value of `?α`,
which thereby determines what `?α` should be.

This expresses that in a term like `a ∈ s`, `s` might be a `Set α` or
`List α` or some other type with a membership operation, and in each case
the "member" type `α` is determined by looking at the container type.
-/
@[reducible] def outParam (α : Sort u) : Sort u := α

import Foundation.Vorspiel.Vorspiel

/-!
# Logic Symbols

This file defines structure that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$
and their homomorphisms.

## Main Definitions
* `LO.LogicalConnective` is defined so that `LO.LogicalConnective F` is a type that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$.
* `LO.LogicalConnective.Hom` is defined so that `f : F →ˡᶜ G` is a homomorphism from `F` to `G`, i.e.,
a function that preserves logical connectives.

-/

namespace LO

section logicNotation

@[notation_class] class Tilde (α : Type*) where
  tilde : α → α

@[notation_class] class Arrow (α : Type*) where
  arrow : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Wedge (α : Type*) where
  wedge : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Vee (α : Type*) where
  vee : α → α → α

class LogicalConnective (α : Type*)
  extends Top α, Bot α, Tilde α, Arrow α, Wedge α, Vee α

prefix:75 "∼" => Tilde.tilde

infixr:60 " ➝ " => Arrow.arrow

infixr:69 " ⋏ " => Wedge.wedge

infixr:68 " ⋎ " => Vee.vee

attribute [match_pattern]
  Tilde.tilde
  Arrow.arrow
  Wedge.wedge
  Vee.vee

end logicNotation

class DeMorgan (F : Type*) [LogicalConnective F] where
  verum           : ∼(⊤ : F) = ⊥
  falsum          : ∼(⊥ : F) = ⊤
  imply (φ ψ : F) : (φ ➝ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ψ
  and (φ ψ : F)   : ∼(φ ⋏ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ∼ψ
  or (φ ψ : F)    : ∼(φ ⋎ ψ) = ∼φ ⋏ ∼ψ
  neg (φ : F)     : ∼∼φ = φ

attribute [simp] DeMorgan.verum DeMorgan.falsum DeMorgan.and DeMorgan.or DeMorgan.neg

/-- Introducing `∼φ` as an abbreviation of `φ ➝ ⊥`. -/
class NegAbbrev (F : Type*) [Tilde F] [Arrow F] [Bot F] where
  neg {φ : F} : ∼φ = φ ➝ ⊥

@[match_pattern] def iff (a b : α) := (a ➝ b) ⋏ (b ➝ a)

C1_dependencies.name: outParam
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
Gadget for marking output parameters in type classes.

For example, the `Membership` class is defined as:
```
class Membership (α : outParam (Type u)) (γ : Type v)
```
This means that whenever a typeclass goal of the form `Membership ?α ?γ` comes
up, Lean will wait to solve it until `?γ` is known, but then it will run
typeclass inference, and take the first solution it finds, for any value of `?α`,
which thereby determines what `?α` should be.

This expresses that in a term like `a ∈ s`, `s` might be a `Set α` or
`List α` or some other type with a membership operation, and in each case
the "member" type `α` is determined by looking at the container type.
-/
@[reducible] def outParam (α : Sort u) : Sort u := α

informal_statement: The `disj` operation on a list of formulas combines the elements using the `∃` logical quantifier in an n-ary fashion, recursively applying ` disj` to the tail of the list and combining the current formula with the result using the logical OR operator `∨`.
informal_proof:
To formalize the definition of the `disj` operation, consider a list `F` of formulas. We define `disj : List F → F` as follows:

- If the list is empty (`[]`), then `disj [] = ⊥`, where `⊥` represents falsity.
- If the list contains a single formula `[φ]`, then `disj [φ] = φ`.
- If the list has multiple formulas `[φ, ψ, ...]`, then `disj [φ, ψ, ...] = φ ∨ disj [ψ, ...]`.

This recursive definition ensures that each formula is combined with the disjunction of all subsequent formulas in the list. By associativity of the `∨` operator, the order in which the disjunctions are evaluated does not affect the final result.

Moreover, since `disj [φ] = φ` and the definition avoids spacing ` disj` in front of the last formula when the list has more than one formula, it maintains consistency with logical disjunction.

This operational definition aligns with natural logical language usage when phrasing an n-ary disjunction, ensuring that the operation is both intuitive and systematically defined for all list lengths.

/-!
# Logic Symbols

This file defines structure that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$
and their homomorphisms.

## Main Definitions
* `LO.LogicalConnective` is defined so that `LO.LogicalConnective F` is a type that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$.
* `LO.LogicalConnective.Hom` is defined so that `f : F →ˡᶜ G` is a homomorphism from `F` to `G`, i.e.,
a function that preserves logical connectives.

-/

namespace LO

section logicNotation

@[notation_class] class Tilde (α : Type*) where
  tilde : α → α

@[notation_class] class Arrow (α : Type*) where
  arrow : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Wedge (α : Type*) where
  wedge : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Vee (α : Type*) where
  vee : α → α → α

class LogicalConnective (α : Type*)
  extends Top α, Bot α, Tilde α, Arrow α, Wedge α, Vee α

prefix:75 "∼" => Tilde.tilde

infixr:60 " ➝ " => Arrow.arrow

infixr:69 " ⋏ " => Wedge.wedge

infixr:68 " ⋎ " => Vee.vee

attribute [match_pattern]
  Tilde.tilde
  Arrow.arrow
  Wedge.wedge
  Vee.vee

end logicNotation

class DeMorgan (F : Type*) [LogicalConnective F] where
  verum           : ∼(⊤ : F) = ⊥
  falsum          : ∼(⊥ : F) = ⊤
  imply (φ ψ : F) : (φ ➝ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ψ
  and (φ ψ : F)   : ∼(φ ⋏ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ∼ψ
  or (φ ψ : F)    : ∼(φ ⋎ ψ) = ∼φ ⋏ ∼ψ
  neg (φ : F)     : ∼∼φ = φ

attribute [simp] DeMorgan.verum DeMorgan.falsum DeMorgan.and DeMorgan.or DeMorgan.neg

/-- Introducing `∼φ` as an abbreviation of `φ ➝ ⊥`. -/
class NegAbbrev (F : Type*) [Tilde F] [Arrow F] [Bot F] where
  neg {φ : F} : ∼φ = φ ➝ ⊥
-- attribute [simp] NegAbbrev.neg

namespace LogicalConnective

section
variable {α : Type*} [LogicalConnective α]

@[match_pattern] def iff (a b : α) := (a ➝ b) ⋏ (b ➝ a)

infix:61 " ⭤ " => LogicalConnective.iff

end

instance PropLogicSymbols : LogicalConnective Prop where
  top := True
  bot := False
  tilde := Not
  arrow := fun P Q => (P → Q)
  wedge := And

@[simp] lemma Prop.iff_eq (φ ψ : Prop) : (φ ⭤ ψ) = (φ ↔ ψ) := by simp[LogicalConnective.iff, iff_iff_implies_and_implies]

informal_statement: For any element `a` and any non-empty list `as`, the conjunction of `a` and all elements in `as` is the same as the conjunction of `a` and the conjunction of `as`.
informal_proof:
We will prove this statement by induction on the list `as`.

**Base Case**: When `as` is a singleton list, i.e., `as = [b]` for some element `b`, we have:
- `conj₂ a [b]` is equivalent to `a ∧ b`.
- `a ∧ ⋀[b]` is also equivalent to `a ∧ b`.
Thus, the base case holds.

**Inductive Step**: Assume the statement holds for a list `rs`. That is, assume:
\[ \text{conj₂}\,a\,rs = a \land \bigwedge rs \]
Now consider the list `cons \psi\ rs`, which is `[ \psi ] \oplus rs`.
- By definition, `conj₂ a (cons \psi\ rs)` is equivalent to `a \land \psi \land \bigwedge rs`.
- This can be rewritten as `a \land (\psi \land \bigwedge rs)`, which is the same as `a \land \text{conj₂}\, \psi\ rs`.

Since the statement holds for `[ \psi ] \oplus rs`, by the principle of induction, it holds for all non-empty lists `as`.

Thus, the theorem is proven.

informal_statement: For all propositions \( a \) and \( b \), \( a \land b \) is equivalent to \( b \land a \).
informal_proof:
First, we consider arbitrary propositions \( a \) and \( b \) and aim to show that \( a \land b \) is equivalent to \( b \land a \).

We break this down into two parts: proving that \( a \land b \) implies \( b \land a \), and vice versa.

1. **Forward Direction (\( a \land b \) implies \( b \land a \))**:
   - Assume \( a \land b \) is true. By definition of conjunction, both \( a \) and \( b \) must be true.
   - Therefore, \( b \) is true and \( a \) is true, which means \( b \land a \) is also true.

2. **Reverse Direction (\( b \land a \) implies \( a \land b \))**:
   - Similarly, assume \( b \land a \) is true. This means both \( b \) and \( a \) are true.
   - Therefore, \( a \) is true and \( b \) is true, which means \( a \land b \) is also true.

Since both directions hold, we conclude that \( a \land b \) is equivalent to \( b \land a \).

# Logic Symbols

This file defines structure that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$
and their homomorphisms.

## Main Definitions
* `LO.LogicalConnective` is defined so that `LO.LogicalConnective F` is a type that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$.
* `LO.LogicalConnective.Hom` is defined so that `f : F →ˡᶜ G` is a homomorphism from `F` to `G`, i.e.,
a function that preserves logical connectives.

-/

  tilde : α → α

@[notation_class] class Arrow (α : Type*) where
  arrow : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Wedge (α : Type*) where
  wedge : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Vee (α : Type*) where
  vee : α → α → α

class LogicalConnective (α : Type*)
  extends Top α, Bot α, Tilde α, Arrow α, Wedge α, Vee α

  or (φ ψ : F)    : ∼(φ ⋎ ψ) = ∼φ ⋏ ∼ψ
  neg (φ : F)     : ∼∼φ = φ

attribute [simp] DeMorgan.verum DeMorgan.falsum DeMorgan.and DeMorgan.or DeMorgan.neg

/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a
C1_dependencies.compilationAlias:

`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in

-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

/-!
# Logic Symbols

This file defines structure that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$
and their homomorphisms.

## Main Definitions
* `LO.LogicalConnective` is defined so that `LO.LogicalConnective F` is a type that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$.
* `LO.LogicalConnective.Hom` is defined so that `f : F →ˡᶜ G` is a homomorphism from `F` to `G`, i.e.,
a function that preserves logical connectives.

-/

namespace LO

section logicNotation

@[notation_class] class Tilde (α : Type*) where
  tilde : α → α

@[notation_class] class Arrow (α : Type*) where

import Foundation.Vorspiel.Vorspiel

/-!
# Logic Symbols

This file defines structure that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$
and their homomorphisms.

## Main Definitions
* `LO.LogicalConnective` is defined so that `LO.LogicalConnective F` is a type that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$.
* `LO.LogicalConnective.Hom` is defined so that `f : F →ˡᶜ G` is a homomorphism from `F` to `G`, i.e.,
a function that preserves logical connectives.

-/

namespace LO

section logicNotation

@[notation_class] class Tilde (α : Type*) where
  tilde : α → α

@[notation_class] class Arrow (α : Type*) where
  arrow : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Wedge (α : Type*) where
  wedge : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Vee (α : Type*) where
  vee : α → α → α

class LogicalConnective (α : Type*)
  extends Top α, Bot α, Tilde α, Arrow α, Wedge α, Vee α

prefix:75 "∼" => Tilde.tilde

infixr:60 " ➝ " => Arrow.arrow

infixr:69 " ⋏ " => Wedge.wedge

infixr:68 " ⋎ " => Vee.vee

attribute [match_pattern]
  Tilde.tilde
  Arrow.arrow
  Wedge.wedge
  Vee.vee

end logicNotation

class DeMorgan (F : Type*) [LogicalConnective F] where
  verum           : ∼(⊤ : F) = ⊥
  falsum          : ∼(⊥ : F) = ⊤
  imply (φ ψ : F) : (φ ➝ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ψ
  and (φ ψ : F)   : ∼(φ ⋏ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ∼ψ
  or (φ ψ : F)    : ∼(φ ⋎ ψ) = ∼φ ⋏ ∼ψ
  neg (φ : F)     : ∼∼φ = φ

attribute [simp] DeMorgan.verum DeMorgan.falsum DeMorgan.and DeMorgan.or DeMorgan.neg

class NegAbbrev (F : Type*) [Tilde F] [Arrow F] [Bot F] where
  neg {φ : F} : ∼φ = φ ➝ ⊥
-- attribute [simp] NegAbbrev.neg

@[match_pattern] def iff (a b : α) := (a ➝ b) ⋏ (b ➝ a)

instance PropLogicSymbols : LogicalConnective Prop where
  top := True

@[simp] lemma Prop.top_eq : ⊤ = True := rfl

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a
C1_dependencies.compilationAlias:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

/-!
# Logic Symbols

This file defines structure that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$
and their homomorphisms.

## Main Definitions
* `LO.LogicalConnective` is defined so that `LO.LogicalConnective F` is a type that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$.
* `LO.LogicalConnective.Hom` is defined so that `f : F →ˡᶜ G` is a homomorphism from `F` to `G`, i.e.,
a function that preserves logical connectives.

-/

namespace LO

section logicNotation

@[notation_class] class Tilde (α : Type*) where
  tilde : α → α

@[notation_class] class Arrow (α : Type*) where
  arrow : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Wedge (α : Type*) where
  wedge : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Vee (α : Type*) where
  vee : α → α → α

class LogicalConnective (α : Type*)
  extends Top α, Bot α, Tilde α, Arrow α, Wedge α, Vee α

prefix:75 "∼" => Tilde.tilde

infixr:60 " ➝ " => Arrow.arrow

infixr:69 " ⋏ " => Wedge.wedge

infixr:68 " ⋎ " => Vee.vee

attribute [match_pattern]
  Tilde.tilde
  Arrow.arrow
  Wedge.wedge
  Vee.vee

end logicNotation

class DeMorgan (F : Type*) [LogicalConnective F] where
  verum           : ∼(⊤ : F) = ⊥
  falsum          : ∼(⊥ : F) = ⊤
  imply (φ ψ : F) : (φ ➝ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ψ
  and (φ ψ : F)   : ∼(φ ⋏ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ∼ψ
  or (φ ψ : F)    : ∼(φ ⋎ ψ) = ∼φ ⋏ ∼ψ
  neg (φ : F)     : ∼∼φ = φ

attribute [simp] DeMorgan.verum DeMorgan.falsum DeMorgan.and DeMorgan.or DeMorgan.neg

class NegAbbrev (F : Type*) [Tilde F] [Arrow F] [Bot F] where
  neg {φ : F} : ∼φ = φ ➝ ⊥
-- attribute [simp] NegAbbrev.neg

@[match_pattern] def iff (a b : α) := (a ➝ b) ⋏ (b ➝ a)

instance PropLogicSymbols : LogicalConnective Prop where
  top := True

  tilde := Not

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a
C1_dependencies.compilationAlias:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

# Logic Symbols

This file defines structure that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$
and their homomorphisms.

## Main Definitions
* `LO.LogicalConnective` is defined so that `LO.LogicalConnective F` is a type that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$.
* `LO.LogicalConnective.Hom` is defined so that `f : F →ˡᶜ G` is a homomorphism from `F` to `G`, i.e.,
a function that preserves logical connectives.

-/

  tilde : α → α

@[notation_class] class Arrow (α : Type*) where
  arrow : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Wedge (α : Type*) where
  wedge : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Vee (α : Type*) where
  vee : α → α → α

class LogicalConnective (α : Type*)
  extends Top α, Bot α, Tilde α, Arrow α, Wedge α, Vee α

  imply (φ ψ : F) : (φ ➝ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ψ

  or (φ ψ : F)    : ∼(φ ⋎ ψ) = ∼φ ⋏ ∼ψ

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a
C1_dependencies.compilationAlias:

informal_statement: For any two lists l₁ and l₂, the combined list l₁ ++ l₂ is disjoint if and only if both l₁ and l₂ are individually disjoint, and their heads are distinct.
informal_proof:
We prove this statement by induction on both lists l₁ and l₂.

**Base Case:**
- **l₁ = [] (empty list):**
  - If l₁ is empty, then l₁ ++ l₂ = l₂.
  - f (l₁ ++ l₂).disj simplifies to f (l₂).disj.
  - The right-hand side, f (l₁.disj ⋎ l₂.disj), simplifies to f (⊥ ⋎ l₂.disj), since l₁ is empty and l₁.disj is false (⊥ represents false).
  - Since ⊥ ⋎ P simplifies to P, the right-hand side further simplifies to f (l₂).disj, matching the left-hand side.
  
- **l₂ = [] (empty list):**
  - Similarly, if l₂ is empty, then l₁ ++ l₂ = l₁.
  - f (l₁ ++ l₂).disj simplifies to f (l₁).disj.
  - The right-hand side, f (l₁.disj ⋎ l₂.disj), simplifies to f (l₁.disj ⋎ ⊥), since l₂ is empty and l₂.disj is false.
  - Since P ⋎ ⊥ simplifies to P, the right-hand side further simplifies to f (l₁).disj, matching the left-hand side.

**Inductive Step:**
Assume the property holds for all lists smaller than l₁ ++ l₂, i.e., for any lists l₁' and l₂' where the length of l₁' or l₂' is less than l₁ ++ l₂.

- **l₁ has a head element a, and l₁' is the tail of l₁ (l₁ = [a] ++ l₁')**
- **l₂ has a head element b, and l₂' is the tail of l₂ (l₂ = [b] ++ l₂')**

We consider the relationship between a and b:

1. **Case 1: a ≠ b**
   - If a ≠ b, then the combined list [a, l₁ ++ b, l₂'] will have distinct heads.
   - By the inductive hypothesis, the disjointedness of l₁ and l₂' implies the disjointedness of l₁ ++ l₂'.
   - Combining this with a ≠ b ensures that the combined list l₁ ++ l₂ is disjoint.
   - Thus, f (l₁ ++ l₂).disj holds, and since a ≠ b, the right-hand side f (l₁.disj ⋎ l₂.disj) also holds.

2. **Case 2: a = b**
   - If a = b, then appending l₁ to l₂ would result in [a, l₁ ++ l₂'], which has a duplicated head.
   - Therefore, the combined list l₁ ++ l₂ is not disjoint.
   - On the right-hand side, since a = b, l₁(disj) ⋎ l₂(disj) would evaluate to false ⋎ false, which is false.
   - Thus, f (l₁ ++ l₂).disj does not hold, and f (l₁.disj ⋎ l₂.disj) also does not hold.

Since in both cases the property holds, the lemma is proven by induction and the use of aesop to generalize the proof across all possible lists.

import Foundation.Vorspiel.Vorspiel

/-!
# Logic Symbols

This file defines structure that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$
and their homomorphisms.

## Main Definitions
* `LO.LogicalConnective` is defined so that `LO.LogicalConnective F` is a type that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$.
* `LO.LogicalConnective.Hom` is defined so that `f : F →ˡᶜ G` is a homomorphism from `F` to `G`, i.e.,
a function that preserves logical connectives.

-/

namespace LO

section logicNotation

@[notation_class] class Tilde (α : Type*) where
  tilde : α → α

@[notation_class] class Arrow (α : Type*) where
  arrow : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Wedge (α : Type*) where
  wedge : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Vee (α : Type*) where
  vee : α → α → α

class LogicalConnective (α : Type*)
  extends Top α, Bot α, Tilde α, Arrow α, Wedge α, Vee α

class DeMorgan (F : Type*) [LogicalConnective F] where

import Foundation.Vorspiel.Vorspiel

/-!
# Logic Symbols

This file defines structure that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$
and their homomorphisms.

## Main Definitions
* `LO.LogicalConnective` is defined so that `LO.LogicalConnective F` is a type that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$.
* `LO.LogicalConnective.Hom` is defined so that `f : F →ˡᶜ G` is a homomorphism from `F` to `G`, i.e.,
a function that preserves logical connectives.

-/

namespace LO

section logicNotation

@[notation_class] class Tilde (α : Type*) where
  tilde : α → α

@[notation_class] class Arrow (α : Type*) where
  arrow : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Wedge (α : Type*) where
  wedge : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Vee (α : Type*) where
  vee : α → α → α

class LogicalConnective (α : Type*)
  extends Top α, Bot α, Tilde α, Arrow α, Wedge α, Vee α

prefix:75 "∼" => Tilde.tilde

infixr:60 " ➝ " => Arrow.arrow

infixr:69 " ⋏ " => Wedge.wedge

infixr:68 " ⋎ " => Vee.vee

attribute [match_pattern]
  Tilde.tilde
  Arrow.arrow
  Wedge.wedge
  Vee.vee

end logicNotation

class DeMorgan (F : Type*) [LogicalConnective F] where
  verum           : ∼(⊤ : F) = ⊥
  falsum          : ∼(⊥ : F) = ⊤
  imply (φ ψ : F) : (φ ➝ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ψ
  and (φ ψ : F)   : ∼(φ ⋏ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ∼ψ
  or (φ ψ : F)    : ∼(φ ⋎ ψ) = ∼φ ⋏ ∼ψ
  neg (φ : F)     : ∼∼φ = φ

attribute [simp] DeMorgan.verum DeMorgan.falsum DeMorgan.and DeMorgan.or DeMorgan.neg

/-- Introducing `∼φ` as an abbreviation of `φ ➝ ⊥`. -/
class NegAbbrev (F : Type*) [Tilde F] [Arrow F] [Bot F] where
  neg {φ : F} : ∼φ = φ ➝ ⊥
-- attribute [simp] NegAbbrev.neg

namespace LogicalConnective

section
variable {α : Type*} [LogicalConnective α]

@[match_pattern] def iff (a b : α) := (a ➝ b) ⋏ (b ➝ a)

infix:61 " ⭤ " => LogicalConnective.iff

end

@[reducible]
instance PropLogicSymbols : LogicalConnective Prop where
  top := True
  bot := False
  tilde := Not
  arrow := fun P Q => (P → Q)
  wedge := And
  vee := Or

@[simp] lemma Prop.top_eq : ⊤ = True := rfl

@[simp] lemma Prop.bot_eq : ⊥ = False := rfl
annotation: @[simp] lemma Prop.bot_eq : ⊥ = False := rfl

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a
C1_dependencies.compilationAlias:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

informal_statement: Map distributes over disjunction: For any function `f` that maps elements of a list `l` to propositions, the disjunction of `f` applied to each element of `l` is equivalent to the existence of an element `a` in `l` such that `f a` holds.
informal_proof:
To prove that `f l.disj` is equivalent to `∃ a ∈ l, f a`, we will consider two cases: when `l` is empty and when `l` contains elements.

1. **Base case:** When `l` is empty, `f l.disj` simplifies to `false` since there are no elements to apply `f` to. Similarly, `∃ a ∈ l, f a` is `false` because there are no elements in `l`. Thus, both sides are equal in this case.

2. **Inductive step:** Assume the equivalence holds for a list `l`. We need to show it holds for `a :: l` (a list with element `a` followed by elements of `l`).

   - On the left side: `f (a :: l).disj` becomes `f a || f l.disj`.
   - By the inductive hypothesis: `f l.disj` is equivalent to `∃ b ∈ l, f b`.
   - Therefore, `f a || ∃ b ∈ l, f b` is equivalent to `∃ a ∈ (a :: l), f a`.

Since both conditions hold, the equivalence is proven by induction.

import Foundation.Vorspiel.Vorspiel

/-!
# Logic Symbols

This file defines structure that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$
and their homomorphisms.

## Main Definitions
* `LO.LogicalConnective` is defined so that `LO.LogicalConnective F` is a type that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$.
* `LO.LogicalConnective.Hom` is defined so that `f : F →ˡᶜ G` is a homomorphism from `F` to `G`, i.e.,
a function that preserves logical connectives.

-/

namespace LO

section logicNotation

@[notation_class] class Tilde (α : Type*) where
  tilde : α → α

@[notation_class] class Arrow (α : Type*) where
  arrow : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Wedge (α : Type*) where
  wedge : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Vee (α : Type*) where
  vee : α → α → α

class LogicalConnective (α : Type*)
  extends Top α, Bot α, Tilde α, Arrow α, Wedge α, Vee α

prefix:75 "∼" => Tilde.tilde

  Arrow.arrow
  Wedge.wedge
  Vee.vee

end logicNotation

class DeMorgan (F : Type*) [LogicalConnective F] where
  verum           : ∼(⊤ : F) = ⊥
  falsum          : ∼(⊥ : F) = ⊤
  imply (φ ψ : F) : (φ ➝ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ψ
  and (φ ψ : F)   : ∼(φ ⋏ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ∼ψ
  or (φ ψ : F)    : ∼(φ ⋎ ψ) = ∼φ ⋏ ∼ψ
  neg (φ : F)     : ∼∼φ = φ

attribute [simp] DeMorgan.verum DeMorgan.falsum DeMorgan.and DeMorgan.or DeMorgan.neg

class NegAbbrev (F : Type*) [Tilde F] [Arrow F] [Bot F] where
  neg {φ : F} : ∼φ = φ ➝ ⊥
-- attribute [simp] NegAbbrev.neg

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a
C1_dependencies.compilationAlias:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

informal_statement: For any type α, and any element a of type α and any list as of elements of type α, the operation disj applied to the list formed by adding element a to the front of as is equal to the disjunction of a with the disj of as.
informal_proof: The lemma establishes a fundamental property of the disj operation on lists. By definition, disj (a :: as) constructs a combined value that includes element a and the result of disj as. Conversely, a ⋎ as(disj) explicitly combines a with the outcome of disj as. Since both expressions are constructed in the same manner and follow identical definitions, they are definitionally equal. This equality is confirmed by the rfl tactic in Lean4, which asserts definitional equivalence.

/-!
# Logic Symbols

This file defines structure that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$
and their homomorphisms.

## Main Definitions
* `LO.LogicalConnective` is defined so that `LO.LogicalConnective F` is a type that has logical connectives $\top, \bot, \land, \lor, \to, \lnot$.
* `LO.LogicalConnective.Hom` is defined so that `f : F →ˡᶜ G` is a homomorphism from `F` to `G`, i.e.,
a function that preserves logical connectives.

-/

namespace LO

section logicNotation

@[notation_class] class Tilde (α : Type*) where
  tilde : α → α

@[notation_class] class Arrow (α : Type*) where
  arrow : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Wedge (α : Type*) where
  wedge : α → α → α

@[notation_class] class Vee (α : Type*) where
  vee : α → α → α

class LogicalConnective (α : Type*)
  extends Top α, Bot α, Tilde α, Arrow α, Wedge α, Vee α

prefix:75 "∼" => Tilde.tilde

  Arrow.arrow

  Vee.vee

end logicNotation

  verum           : ∼(⊤ : F) = ⊥
  falsum          : ∼(⊥ : F) = ⊤
  imply (φ ψ : F) : (φ ➝ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ψ
  and (φ ψ : F)   : ∼(φ ⋏ ψ) = ∼φ ⋎ ∼ψ
  or (φ ψ : F)    : ∼(φ ⋎ ψ) = ∼φ ⋏ ∼ψ
  neg (φ : F)     : ∼∼φ = φ

attribute [simp] DeMorgan.verum DeMorgan.falsum DeMorgan.and DeMorgan.or DeMorgan.neg

class NegAbbrev (F : Type*) [Tilde F] [Arrow F] [Bot F] where
  neg {φ : F} : ∼φ = φ ➝ ⊥
-- attribute [simp] NegAbbrev.neg

/--
`Not p`, or `¬p`, is the negation of `p`. It is defined to be `p → False`,
so if your goal is `¬p` you can use `intro h` to turn the goal into
`h : p ⊢ False`, and if you have `hn : ¬p` and `h : p` then `hn h : False`
and `(hn h).elim` will prove anything.
For more information: [Propositional Logic](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/propositions_and_proofs.html#propositional-logic)
-/
def Not (a : Prop) : Prop := a → False

informal_statement: The exclusive disjunction (XOR) of a proposition with an empty list results in falsity.
informal_proof: Since there are no elements in the list to which the proposition can be exclusively disjuncted, the result is inherently falsity. This aligns with the understanding that an exclusive OR operation requires at least one true value to result in true, and in the absence of any operands, the outcome must logically be falsity.
